lesson.title: Collapse of a Superpower: The Soviet Union Dissolves
lesson.summary: Less than two years after the Berlin Wall fell, a failed hardline coup against Gorbachev accelerated the collapse of Soviet authority, and by the end of December 1991 the Soviet Union had ceased to exist, replaced by fifteen independent nations.
lesson.body:
The fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989 and the collapse of communist governments across Eastern Europe that followed put enormous pressure on the Soviet Union itself. Nationalist and independence movements grew rapidly in Soviet republics that had long chafed under Moscow's control, especially the Baltic states of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, which had been forcibly annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940 and pushed hardest for independence as Gorbachev's reforms opened political space that had not existed before.

Gorbachev himself was caught between two pressures he could not fully reconcile: reformers and nationalists who wanted faster change and more independence for the republics, and hardline communists within the Communist Party and military who blamed his reforms for undermining Soviet power and unity. That hardline faction attempted to seize control in August 1991, placing Gorbachev under house arrest at his vacation home in Crimea and declaring a state of emergency in what became known as the August Coup. The coup collapsed within three days, defeated largely by public resistance in Moscow led by Boris Yeltsin, the popularly elected president of the Russian republic, who climbed atop a tank outside the Russian parliament building to rally opposition to the plotters.

The coup's failure destroyed what remained of the Communist Party's authority and accelerated the very collapse the plotters had hoped to prevent. Republic after republic declared independence in the weeks that followed, and on December 1, 1991, Ukrainian voters approved independence from the Soviet Union in an overwhelming referendum. On December 8, 1991, the leaders of Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus met and signed the Belavezha Accords, formally declaring that the Soviet Union had ceased to exist and establishing a loose Commonwealth of Independent States among most of the former Soviet republics.

Gorbachev, now a president without a country to lead, resigned on December 25, 1991, and the Soviet flag over the Kremlin was lowered for the last time, replaced by the flag of the Russian Federation. By the end of December 1991, the Soviet Union, the superpower that had defined one side of the Cold War for nearly seven decades, had formally dissolved into fifteen independent nations. The peaceful nature of the collapse, given the vast nuclear arsenal involved, surprised many observers who had feared a far more violent ending to the Cold War era that had begun in the years after World War II.
